items.title: 5 Mind-Blowing Blue Whale Facts
items.premise: Did you know that the largest animal to ever live on Earth has a heart the size of a small car? Discover incredible, verifiable facts about the blue whale, from its extreme weight to how far its heartbeat can travel underwater.
facts: Blue whales are the largest animals ever known to exist on Earth, reaching lengths of up to 100 feet (30 meters).
An adult blue whale can weigh up to 200 tons, equivalent to roughly 33 adult elephants.
A blue whale's heart weighs approximately 400 pounds (180 kg), which is roughly the size of a bumper car.
Under optimal ocean conditions, a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected underwater up to 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) away.
The tongue of a full-grown blue whale weighs around 2.7 metric tons, which is heavier than an entire adult female elephant.
Their vocalizations can reach 188 decibels, making them louder than a jet engine taking off at 140 decibels.
A blue whale's sound can travel through ocean waters across distances of up to 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers).
Newborn blue whale calves drink about 100 gallons (380 liters) of rich mother's milk every single day.
During peak summer feeding season, an adult blue whale consumes up to 4 tons (8,000 pounds) of krill daily.
Despite their massive body size, a blue whale's throat is so narrow it cannot swallow anything larger than a beach ball.

items.title: 60 Hours Underwater: The Harrison Okene Rescue
items.premise: In May 2013, a tugboat capsized off the coast of Nigeria and plunged 30 meters to the ocean floor. Cook Harrison Okene survived in pitch-black darkness inside a tiny air pocket for nearly three days before deep-sea divers found him.
facts: On May 26, 2013, the tugboat Jascon-4 capsized in rough ocean swells 20 miles off the coast of Nigeria.
The vessel sank 30 meters (100 feet) beneath the ocean surface to the freezing seabed.
29-year-old ship cook Harrison Okene was trapped inside as water rapidly flooded the vessel.
Okene managed to swim through darkness into an overturned engineer's toilet area containing a 4-foot air pocket.
He spent 60 hours trapped in near-freezing water dressed only in shorts, holding onto a small wooden shelf.
With only one bottle of Coca-Cola, Okene listened to sea creatures scavenge the ship in pitch darkness.
On May 28, 2013, South African rescue divers descended to the wreck believing it was strictly a body recovery mission.
Diver Nico van Heerden reached into the flooded compartment and was shocked when Okene grabbed his hand.
Divers equipped Okene with a diving helmet and warm water suit before guiding him to a diving bell.
Because of extreme nitrogen saturation at 30 meters depth, Okene spent 51 hours in a decompression chamber on the surface.
Harrison Okene was the sole survivor among the 12 crew members onboard the Jascon-4.
